To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) RVs have been associated with human diseases; 2) RVs can be identified in a large number of human populations; and 3) the association between RV and diseases is of rapidly growth interest in understanding genetic mechanisms of both common and complex diseases.

rare genetic variants are important contributors to human diseases, and the association of rare variants with human diseases is an important and challenging research area in the field of human genetics.

(1) the association between RV and disease is more complex and difficult to detect than the association between common variant and disease, and (2) RVs can be detected and analyzed in the same way as common variants, but the statistical power is much lower for rare variants than that for common variants, especially for the rare variants that occur in the coding regions of the genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following three questions.
the development and applications of statistical and computational methods for identifying RVs and associating them with human diseases.
developing statistical and bioinformatics methods for identifying rare variants associated with human diseases, and applying these methods to analyze large-scale genomic data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RVs have been found in both common and rare human diseases, and they are important for the understanding of the etiology of both common and complex diseases.
RVs are associated with human diseases.
rare genetic variants are associated with a wide spectrum of human diseases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are interested in understanding the association between genetic variants and complex traits.
we are trying to develop statistical methods to identify the RVs that are associated with diseases, which is called RV association test.
we have developed and applied several statistical and machine learning approaches to identify the associations between RVs and complex human diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rare variants are more likely to be associated with disease than common variants.
we can now associate RVs with diseases in a genome-wide fashion using a statistical framework called the rare variant association test (RVAT) (Wu, et al., 2011).

the rare variant association tests we developed can detect RV association signals that are missed by the standard tests, and that the RV association test is robust to the violation of rare variant assumption.
